articleTitle: Current conveyors: A review of the state of the art
abstract: A new circuit concept called current conveying was introduced by Smith and Sedra (1968). The current conveyor has since become a basic building block in a variety of instrumentation and communication systems. Its state of the art development is reviewed.

articleTitle: Algebraic formulation of the fast Fourier transform
abstract: A new unified formulation of the fast Fourier transform is presented. It is shown that all FFT algorithms can be derived by different methods of multidimensional array unwrapping. The eight principal decimation in time FFT algorithms are derived. Two algorithms with the desirable properties of sequential input, sequential output and identical computational geometry are also derived. The derivation of the decimation in frequency FFT algorithms is then discussed. While most of the results presented here have been derived earlier using matrix Kronecker products, the present formulation is simpler and more intuitive that the equivalent matrix formulation.

articleTitle: Standard cell approach for generating custom CMOS/SOS devices using a fully automatic layout program
abstract: This paper describes and illustrates the standard cell approach for generating low-cost, quick-turnaround, custom, random logic LSI and VLSI devices using the CMOS/SOS technology. Special features of the automatic layout program that provide increased performance, speed, and density will be highlighted and illustrated in various LSI devices into which these features have been designed.

articleTitle: The potential of biopolar devices in LSI gigabit logic
abstract: The logic swing can be reduced to improve propagation delays without affecting the noise margin due to switching transients. The author proposes a simple differential CML gate with small-geometry bipolar devices which can operate at gigabit logic speeds and at sub mW power levels. It is well suited to compete with GaAs technologies.

Active magnitude compensation methods for the finite bandwidth of operational amplifiers when employed in the differential voltage controlled voltage source structures are given. The results are summarized in a table.

Josephson devices combine high speed and low power dissipation which are desirable assets necessary but not sufficient to guarantee the realization of high performance computers. Adequate gain, margins and other engineering considerations also must be achieved in circuit and system designs. The evolution of random logic circuits is an example used to illustrate how this has been done, and two new DC powered logic approaches are introduced.

articleTitle: Computer-aided design and analysis of standard IIR architectures: Part I
abstract: Presents a computer-aided design procedure for the popular direct, cascade, parallel, normal, Gray-Markel, and Wave IIR digital filter architectures. These architectures are developed within a common state variable format. Using linear algebraic techniques, the computer-derived filters are analyzed in terms of register overflow and roundoff metrics. In this part the fundamental problem and objectives are outlined. Overflow and roundoff errors, in a state-determined filter, are analyzed and formulated for computer-aided analysis.

The Automated Universal Array system is a new, minimum-cost approach to generating custom LSI devices. It incorporates a specially developed fixed geometry design with an automatic layout program. With this system, custom LSI devices can be produced by generation of a single unique metal level, with the interconnections determined and optimized automatically. This paper describes the topological design of the AUA chip and the effectiveness of the fully automatic layout program.

I am very pleased that the Newsletter and Magazine Editors of Division I have invited the Director candidates to communicate with the members of Division I. A little research and some guessing suggests that among the 34,000 memberships in our four societies (ASSP, CAS, CS, IT) there are 33% outside the U.S. and 25,000 people in all since some of us hold membership in more than one Division I Society. About 25% of us also subscribe to the IEEE Proceedings. Our Division tends to be strongly technically oriented with substantial interest in theoretical aspects of our fields. I believe this strong interest in technical matters is the main reason we belong to Division I Societies.

articleTitle: An algorithm for “8275 Programmable CRT Controller” timing
abstract: An algorithm is developed to determine the `8275 Programmable CRT Controller' timing parameters for a given CRT monitor requirements and the desired display format. This algorithm has been implemented in BASIC language and executed on the TRS-80 computer. There may not always exist a set of 8275 parameters satisfying simultaneously the monitor and display format requirements. This is allowed for by leaving the choice of modifications in requirements to the programmer. When the choice of modification in requirements works out to be obvious, program execution continues after indicating to the programmer the decision taken. The flow chart and the program are shown.

articleTitle: The first IEEE International Conference on Circuits and Computer (ICCC 80)
abstract: The first IEEE International Conference on Circuits and Computers, (ICCC 80) was held at the Rye Town Hilton Inn, in Port Chester, New York between October 1–3, 1980. The total number of attendees was about 1,200. The total number of papers presented was about 270 from authors from 30 countries. The industry attendance was over 70 percent of the total. For a first conference, ICCC 80 was a great success. As a matter of record I was told that no IEEE Conference had reached 1,200 at their first meeting. The subject of VLSI was a major factor in the success of ICCC 80.

articleTitle: Combined photovoltaic/thermal solar array DC electrical model
abstract: An electrical model of a combined photovoltaic/thermal solar array has been developed to predict the steady state behavior of the line currents, power output and array voltage. The effects of temperature on the solar cell characteristics is included in the analysis. The model includes line isolation diodes and `open cell' bypass diodes. A numerical procedure based on the Contraction Mapping Fixed Point Theorem is used to solve the associated nonlinear equations.

The Computer Aided Network Design (CANDE) subcommittee of the Circuits and Systems Society was involved in a number of activities during 1980. These activities supported the basic charter of providing a forum for supporting the investigation and discussion of topics associated with the use of computer aids in the design, analysis, and verification of electrical circuit design with emphasis on LSI and VLSI circuits.

articleTitle: On comparing hardware implementations of fixed point digital filters
abstract: Distributed arithmetic structures are an alternative to the use of conventional multipliers in hardware implementations of digital filters. The authors compare the various methods of using distributed arithmetic in implementing fixed point digital filters. They introduce as a measure of hardware complexity the chip area needed to fabricate competing designs using nMOS technology. Comparisons of alternate realizations in hardware are also made. These comparisons are based on equating the output signal quality of each design. They show that traditional measures of complexity (such as the number of multipliers per output sample) do not agree with complexity measures based on chip area.

The 1981 Program Plan of the USAB (Revised May 1) came in the mail earlier this summer. It gives detailed information on USAB organization and operations, plus budgetary and staffing lists, some of which I feel that I should pass on to you. Indeed, I have an impression from conversations and (a few) written communications that I have had with some of you, that the Society membership at large is not that well acquainted with what the USAB Professional Activities (PA) program is all about. Some quotes from the 1981 Program Plan should answer some of the questions I have been asked about the mandate and commitment of the USAB and should also, I trust, be of general interest to all of you.

Since the time of my last report to you, the Circuits and Systems Society has held its annual symposium in Chicago. This Symposium was highly successful and the Society owes a debt of gratitude to Ben Leon and Mac Van Valkenburg, who served as Co-Chairmen of the 1981 ISCAS. Special thanks are also due to Tom Trick who put together an outstanding technical program with an appropriate mixture of invited and contributed sessions. Each of the sessions had the right balance between theoretically oriented papers and those with a practical bent. The sessions were well-attended and very stimulating. There is no question that this conference extends the Circuits and Systems Society's tradition of having a high-quality, well-organized conference. For those of you who were unable to attend, the Conference Proceedings may be ordered through headquarters (IEEE Catalog No. 81CH1635–2).

I would like to begin this column by expressing my deep appreciation, on behalf of the Circuits and Systems Society, to Carl Kurth for serving as President of the Circuits and Systems Society during this past year. Through Carl's leadership our Society was able to bring into focus some areas of future growth and to develop a strategy to implement this growth. We all hope that Carl will continue to provide us with his wise counsel and advice.

In my last column I indicated that I would report to you on issues which were discussed at the June Technical Activities Board (TAB) meeting. There are two items that I think may be of specific interest to our Society's members: the possible restructuring of the divisions within TAB, and the relatively small number of nominations made for major IEEE awards.

The article on Bipolar Gigabit Logic in Vol. 3, No. 1 by S. G. Knorr shows a circuit virtually identical to one first published by J. S. Brothers and myself in the 1968 ISSCC Conference. Plessey have built digital synthesizer chips based on such circuits for some ten years achieving toggle rates well into the gigabit range. It seems this work was so early that it has been forgotten and is now being reinvented. TOSHIBA gave an almost identical paper at last year's IEDM.

I'd like to devote most of this column to the November 4th meeting of the Circuits and Systems Society Administrative Committee. The most significant actions taken were constitutional changes aimed at strengthening the operation of our Society by providing for added continuity in the areas of publications and conferences. Specifically, a new conference committee was formally organized with a chairperson, who would serve usually for a two- to three-year term, chosen by the president. Members of this committee would include the immediate past conference chairperson (both of the Circuits and Systems Symposium and the International Conference on Circuits and Computers), and the pending conference chairperson for the next two years. This committee would review requests for future conference sites, and, most importantly, act as an advisory body for conference chairpersons. In the past, conference responsibilities resided with the president-elect. However, since the president-elect only served a one-year term, there was little continuity. Ming Liou is currently chairperson of this committee.

This issue of Circuits and Systems is the first of several featuring papers originally presented at last fall's extremely successful International Conference on Circuits and Computers. One is co-authored by Al Feller, Dick Noto and Allan Smith, and the other by Dick Noto, Fred Borgini and Barry Suskind.

In his book Fundamentals of Network Analysis, Professor Hostetter attempts to present the basic techniques of circuit analysis in a form suitable for a one-semester or one-quarter undergraduate course. The author states in the preface that the book is a response to pressure that has built up over the past several years to condense some of the more traditional two- or three-semester course secquences into a single course. In the specific case of network analysis, the author feels that such an abridgement can be achieved without compromising the students' educational needs.

Wellstead has assembled in this book the basic concepts of network modelling, variational modelling and bond graph methods with energy being the unifying concept. The author acknowledges the fact that he has drawn extensively from (1) introduction to Systems Dynamics by J. L. Shearer, A. T. Murphy and H. H. Richardson, (2) Dynamics of Mechanical and Electromechanical Systems by S. H. Crandall, et al., and (3) Analysis and Design of Engineering Systems by H. M. Paynter. For the purposes of serving as a text, Wellstead's book is disappointing in that it does not provide sufficient discussion and examples in Part 1: Basics and Part 2: Systematic Modelling Methods. For example, the presentations of fundamental concepts by Shearer, et al., and Crandall, et al., as well as that given by K. Ogata in Systems Dynamics, contain considerably more explanation than that given by Wellstead.

In this era of automation, reliability engineering has a special place. The importance of reliability engineering becomes apparent when, in everyday life, we expect on-time transportation, reliable communication, and a steady supply of electric power and other utilities. The complex systems providing these services consist of many components, each one of which must operate properly to ensure reliable system operation.

If anything characterizes this particular issue of Circuits & Systems, it is variety. This number contains two regular feature articles, a special feature, information on IEEE elections, and a larger than usual letters section.

The book summarizes present day knowledge about the analysis and design of active networks. The first three chapters, covering about 20 per cent of the book, are devoted to the review of various ideal network elements and to the analysis. The style of these chapters emphasizes formal definitions. The author chose to analyze practically all networks in his book by manipulations of structures with nullators and norators, and does not rely on standard analysis methods.

Our three features this issue provide us with a great deal of variety. Co-authors Fred Taylor and Jeffrey Marshall present part one of a three-part paper which explores how computer simulation can be an invaluable aid in the design process.
